data.name: Iron Commando - Koutetsu no Senshi
data.detailed_description:
Take control of either Jake, a soldier, or Chang Li, a martial arts master, in your quest to stop G.H.O.S.T. from capturing a radioactive meteorite.
Iron Commando comes to and Steam via Piko Interactive.

10 levels of brawling action with many unique experiences such as riding in a Jeep, mine cart and even a motorcycle. 2 player simultaneous play, stereo sound plus new experiences never experienced in a brawling game before. Punch, kick, shoot and beat your way through the G.H.O.S.T. thugs to get that meteorite back for the good guys.
Fans of Final Fight and Streets of Rage, grab your copy of Iron Commando for the first time, officially, in North America.

reviews.review:
Iron Commando: Koutetsu no Senshi is a relic from the 16-bit era that demonstrates how creative developers could be when working within the limitations of classic hardware. Developed by Arcade Zone and brought to Steam by Piko Interactive, this side-scrolling action game originally appeared in Japan during the final years of the Super Nintendo's lifespan. Although it never achieved the same level of fame as many of its contemporaries, its modern re-release gives players the opportunity to experience a title that embraced excess, variety, and arcade-style spectacle long before such design choices became nostalgic selling points.

The game follows two operatives, Jack and Chang Li, as they pursue a dangerous terrorist group that has stolen a mysterious radioactive meteorite. The storyline is intentionally simple, serving mainly as a vehicle for a fast-paced journey across multiple locations packed with enemies and environmental hazards. While the narrative is hardly groundbreaking, it succeeds in establishing a classic action-movie atmosphere that fits the game's identity. Every stage feels like a new chapter in an over-the-top adventure, ranging from urban battlegrounds to more unusual and unexpected settings that keep players curious about what comes next.

Combat remains the centerpiece of the experience, and Iron Commando makes a notable effort to avoid becoming repetitive. In addition to punches, kicks, and special attacks, players can pick up an assortment of weapons scattered throughout each level. Firearms, melee weapons, and explosives all make appearances, giving encounters a greater sense of unpredictability. The game also frequently changes the formula by introducing vehicle sequences and action segments that break up the standard beat-'em-up structure. These moments may not always be perfectly polished, but they add personality and reinforce the feeling that the developers were constantly trying to surprise the player.

Visually, the game captures the charm of mid-1990s sprite-based design. Character models are colorful, enemy types are diverse, and backgrounds contain enough detail to make each environment memorable. The soundtrack complements the gameplay with energetic tracks that maintain a consistent sense of urgency throughout the campaign. While modern players may notice some dated animations and limited effects compared to contemporary releases, the presentation still carries an undeniable retro appeal that fans of classic gaming will appreciate.

That said, Iron Commando can occasionally feel like a product of its time in less favorable ways. Enemy placement can be overwhelming, and certain sections rely heavily on trial and error. The combat system, while enjoyable, lacks the refinement and mechanical depth found in the genre's most celebrated titles. Some battles drag on longer than necessary due to enemy durability, and the game's overall difficulty may discourage players who are unfamiliar with old-school arcade design principles. Nevertheless, these frustrations are often balanced by the title's willingness to experiment and maintain a brisk pace.

Perhaps Iron Commando's greatest strength is its sense of identity. Rather than attempting to imitate its competitors outright, it embraces a more chaotic and adventurous style. Cooperative play enhances the experience considerably, turning difficult encounters into entertaining moments of teamwork. For enthusiasts interested in exploring overlooked entries in gaming history, the title serves as an excellent example of a hidden gem that deserved more attention than it initially received.

Iron Commando: Koutetsu no Senshi is not a flawless revival of the beat-'em-up genre, but it remains an entertaining and worthwhile excursion into the past. Its combination of varied gameplay, memorable stage design, and unapologetically retro sensibilities gives it a unique place among classic action games. Players willing to overlook some rough edges will discover a spirited adventure that continues to entertain more than three decades after its original debut.

Rating: 6/10
